# Cornell University
Cornell University, founded in 1865 as New York’s land-grant institution, is a prestigious research university with a decentralized structure comprising 16 colleges, including 12 privately endowed and four publicly supported statutory colleges. It operates on a 4–1–4 academic calendar and is designated as a land-, space-, and sea-grant university. Admissions are highly competitive, with a 6.9% acceptance rate for the Class of 2026, and the institution emphasizes diversity and financial aid initiatives to support low-income and first-generation students. Cornell offers a broad range of international programs, including study abroad opportunities across six continents and joint degrees with partner institutions worldwide. Its campuses include notable facilities like the Cornell Tech campus in New York City and the Weill Cornell Medical College in Qatar.
Academically, Cornell is consistently ranked among the top global universities, excelling in architecture, business, and international relations programs. Its library system holds over 10 million items, including operation of the influential arXiv e-print archive. Cornell University Press, one of the oldest in the U.S., publishes extensively across multiple disciplines. As an R1 research university, Cornell reported $1.18 billion in R&D expenditures in 2021, with notable contributions in nuclear physics, space exploration (including Mars missions), automotive safety, and computing technology. The university supports a vibrant student life with over 1,000 organizations, a large fraternity and sorority system, multiple student publications, and robust outdoor education and athletic programs. Notable alumni include heads of state, Nobel laureates, judges, inventors, authors, and entertainers, reflecting its broad impact across fields.
